texts.label: text
texts.orig: In this study, tensile tests of 304 and 316 austenitic stainless steels (ASS) at various strain rates were performed to investigate the strain rate effect on tensile properties. It is shown that the strain rate effect on stress depends not only on the strain rate but also on the plastic strain level. Accordingly, a modification of the existing Johnson-Cook (J-C) model is proposed to incorporate the interacting effect of plastic strain and strain rate for 304 and 316 ASS. The proposed modified J-C model can reduce the difference from the experimental data at various strain levels, compared to the existing J-C model. [DOI: 10.1115/1.4050833]

texts.orig: The Johnson-Cook model is one of the most widely used phenomenological models. This model has been embedded in many commercial FE programs because of its simplicity. It has five material constants and can describe the stress as the multiplications of three terms: plastic strain hardening term [14], strain rate term, and temperature term. Many researchers have modified the terms in the J-C model for more accurate prediction of tensile behaviors under various conditions. Maheshwari et al. [15] modified the temperature term to predict the hot deformation processing of aluminum alloy steel at high temperature. Zhang et al. [16] and Huh and Kang [17] introduced nonlinear strain rate terms (instead of linear term in the J-C model) to predict the stress of aluminum alloy and high strength steel. However, these J-C type models assume that the effect of plastic strain, strain rate, and temperature can be separated and thus is independent with no interacting effect. Some coupled models combining the effect of two or three terms have also been proposed. Hou et al. [18] added a temperature term into the strain hardening term to predict the behavior of titanium alloy in a wide range of temperature. Tan el al. [19] added a plastic strain term into the strain rate effect term to predict the stress of aluminum alloy at high strain rates. Li et al. [20] and Lin et al. [21] combined all effects of plastic strain, strain rate, and temperature to predict the behavior of low alloy steel and Al-Cu-Mg alloy at various strain rate and temperature conditions. As such, the effect of plastic strain, strain rate, and temperature on the stress can be coupled when the range or effect of work hardening, strain rate, and temperature becomes larger.

texts.orig: The hardening behavior of austenitic stainless steels is related to the dislocation interactions, martensite phase transformation, and twinning [22-26]. The contribution of these factors to the hardening behavior depends on various conditions such as chemical composition of the material, strain level, stress state, grain size, strain rate, temperature, and so on [22-26]. As results, the hardening of austenitic stainless steels with high ductility shows complex behaviors due to the competitive influence of these factors. Gupta et al. [27] showed that the original J-C model could not well reflect the dynamic strain aging effect of 304 austenitic stainless steel, and Cadoni et al. [28] showed that the dynamic increase factor (DIF) of the yield and tensile strength is different for 304 material. Kotkunde et al. [29] used the coupled constitutive model to predict the hot deformation behavior of 304 and 316 austenitic stainless steels. For complex material behaviors, it would be clear that a model with the combined effects of plastic strain, strain rate, and temperature can better predict the material behavior. In order to focus to the discussion of the effect of strain rate on stress-strain rate in austenitic stainless steel, the test temperature is fixed on room temperature in this paper.

texts.orig: 2.1 Test Materials. Tensile tests using round bar specimens were performed for 304 and 316 series ASS under various strain rates at room temperature. Table 1 shows chemical compositions of the tested materials (304: JIS G4304 SUS304, 304 L: ASME SA240M TP304L, and 316L: ASME SA312 TP316L). The dimensions of the specimens are shown in Fig. 1. Note that experiments were carried out at three different institutes. Although the experiments were conducted at different institutes, the effect of the different test facility on measured stress-strain curve is believed to be minor, because the experimental and data calibration procedures were based on the standard procedure. For 304 ASS, the strain rate ranged from 0.001/s to 1000/s. The tests from 0.001/s to 0.1/s were carried out using standard tensile testing machine (Shimadzu AG-100kNG, Kyoto, Japan), whereas those from 1/s to 1000/s using high-speed tensile testing machine (Shimadzu HITS-TX). For each strain rate, three tests were performed. For 304 L ASS, the strain rate ranged from 0.001/s to 100/s, and all tests were carried out using high strain rate testing machine (Instron VHS system). For 316 L ASS, the strain rate ranged from 0.0004/s to 10/s. The tests from 0.0004/s to 0.04/s were carried out using universal testing machine (RB 301 Unitech-M), and 1/s and 10/s were carried out using servohydraulic testing machine (Instron 8501). For each strain rate, two tests were performed.

texts.orig: It is known that the hardening behavior of austenitic stainless steels due to plastic deformation is related to the phase transformation of metastable c -austenite to a 0 -martensite (transformationinduced plasticity, TRIP), twinning-induced plasticity, and dislocation interactions [22-26,30-33]. The 304 series stainless steels have the low stability of c -austenite phase, the TRIP effect on hardening behavior dominates. On the other hand, the 316 series stainless steels have the high stability of c -austenite phase, the twinning-induced plasticity effect is more dominant than the TRIP effect [31,32]. In addition, dislocation slip and density of dislocation also affect the hardening behavior. The degree of effect of these factors varies depending not only on chemical composition but also on various conditions such as plastic strain, strain rate, temperature, stress state, and others [22-26,30-32].

texts.orig: In this study, the strain rate effect on tensile properties of three different 304 and 316 series austenitic stainless steels is investigated. Tensile tests are performed at room temperature at the strain rate ranging from 0.001 to 1000/s. With increasing the strain rate, the yield strength increases monotonically, whereas the ultimate tensile strength and uniform elongation decrease first and then increase again.
texts.text: In this study, the strain rate effect on tensile properties of three different 304 and 316 series austenitic stainless steels is investigated. Tensile tests are performed at room temperature at the strain rate ranging from 0.001 to 1000/s. With increasing the strain rate, the yield strength increases monotonically, whereas the ultimate tensile strength and uniform elongation decrease first and then increase again.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: One interesting finding from experimental data is that, for 304 and 316 austenitic stainless steels with high ductility and complex material hardening behavior, the strain rate effect on true stress depends on a plastic strain level, and thus the interacting effect of the strain rate and plastic strain should be considered. Many existing models such as the Johnson-Cook type models, popularly used to characterize the strain effect on tensile properties, assume that the term for the strain rate effect can be separable to the term for the plastic strain, and thus cannot properly incorporate the combined effect of the strain rate and plastic strain. To take this account into consideration, a modified Johnson-Cook model is proposed, where a term including the plastic strain and strain rate is introduced. Compared to the existing Johnson-Cook model, the modified Johnson-Cook model can reduce the errors between the test data and predicted true stress at various strain levels; for instance, the maximum error is reduced from 16.6% to 9.6%.
